L1@P0: GEODESICS IN A GRAPH OF PERFECT MATCHINGS
L2@P0: ROY H. JENNINGS
L3@P0: Abstract. Let Pm be the graph on the set of perfect matchings
L4@P0: in the complete graph K2m, where two perfect matchings are connected by an edge if their symmetric difference is a cycle of length
L5@P0: four. This paper studies geodesics in Pm. The diameter of Pm,
L6@P0: as well as the eccentricity of each vertex, are shown to be m − 1.
L7@P0: Two proofs are given to show that the number of geodesics between any two antipodes is mm−2
L8@P0: . The first is a direct proof via a
L9@P0: recursive formula, and the second is via reduction to the number of
L10@P0: minimal factorizations of a given m-cycle in the symmetric group
L11@P0: Sm. An explicit formula for the number of geodesics between any
L12@P0: two matchings in Pm is also given.
L13@P0: Let Mm be the graph on the set of non-crossing perfect matchings of 2m labeled points on a circle with the same adjacency condition as in Pm. Mm is an induced subgraph of Pm, and it is
L14@P0: shown that Mm has exactly one pair of antipodes having the maximal number mm−2 of geodesics between them.
L15@P0: 1. Introduction
L16@P0: Consider a set of 2m labeled points on a circle. Join its points
L17@P0: in disjoint pairs by m straight line segments, such that no two lines
L18@P0: intersect. Abstractly, this is a perfect matching in the complete graph
L19@P0: K2m. Such a matching is called a non-crossing perfect matching.
L20@P0: Hernando, Hurtado and Noy defined in [8] the graph of non-crossing
L21@P0: perfect matchings Mm, in which two matchings are connected by an
L22@P0: edge if their symmetric difference is a cycle of length four. They showed
L23@P0: that the diameter and the eccentricity of every vertex in this graph are
L24@P0: m − 1.
L25@P0: This paper studies the graph Pm on the set of all perfect matchings
L26@P0: in the complete graph K2m where two matchings are connected by an
L27@P0: edge if their symmetric difference is a cycle of length four.
L28@P0: The distance between any two matchings in Pm is shown to depend
L29@P0: only on the number of components in their union.
L30@P0: Theorem (Theorem 3.4). For any M1, M2 ∈ Pm, d(M1, M2) =

L32@P1: Although Pm is larger than the graph of non-crossing perfect matchings Mm, which is an induced subgraph of Pm, it is shown that the
L33@P1: two graphs still share the same diameter, and that it is equal to the
L34@P1: eccentricity of all of their vertices.
L35@P1: Theorem (Corollary 3.5). The diameter of Pm, as well as the
L36@P1: eccentricity of every vertex in it, is m − 1.
L37@P1: Enumeration of the number of geodesics (shortest paths) between
L38@P1: antipodes in Pm reveals the following surprising result.
L39@P1: Theorem (Corollary 4.5). The number of geodesics between any
L40@P1: two antipodes in Pm is mm−2.
L41@P1: The expression mm−2 appears in Cayley’s well known formula for the
L42@P1: number of labeled trees on m vertices. On the other hand, Hurwitz [9]
L43@P1: (see also [12]) showed that it gives as well the number of factorizations
L44@P1: of a given m-cycle as a product of m − 1 transpositions in Sm. (Bijections between these trees and factorizations appear, e.g., in [7, 11].) In
L45@P1: Section 5, an alternative proof, suggested by Y. Roichman, for Corollary 4.5 is provided via reduction to the number of factorizations of a
L46@P1: given m-cycle as a product of m − 1 transpositions.
L47@P1: An explicit formula for the number of geodesics between any two
L48@P1: matchings in Pm is given in Corollary 4.6.
L49@P1: Corollary 4.5 does not hold for the subgraph Mm. Instead, we have
L50@P1: the following result.
L51@P1: Theorem (Theorem 4.7). The graph Mm of non-crossing perfect
L52@P1: matchings has a unique pair of matchings with mm−2geodesics between
L53@P1: them. All other pairs have a smaller number of geodesics.
L54@P1: This paper is based on the author’s M.Sc. thesis. For generalizations
L55@P1: and extensions of results in this paper see [2, 3, 6].
L56@P1: 2. The Graph of Perfect Matchings
L57@P1: Consider the set of all perfect matchings in the complete graph K2m.
L58@P1: Denote the graph of perfect matchings on this set, in which two

L90@P2: 3. Geodesics and Diameter
L91@P2: Recall that a geodesic between two vertices in a connected graph
L92@P2: is a shortest path between them. The distance between two vertices
L93@P2: u and v, denoted by d(u, v), is the length of a geodesic between them.
L94@P2: The eccentricity of a vertex is the maximal distance between this
L95@P2: vertex and any other vertex. The maximal length of a geodesic in
L96@P2-3: a connected graph is called the graph’s diameter. If the distance4 ROY H. JENNINGS
L97@P3: between two vertices is the graph’s diameter, then the vertices are
L98@P3: called antipodes.

L391@P7: 5. Factorization of Permutations by Transpositions
L392@P7: Let Sm be the symmetric group on m elements. A minimal factorization by transpositions (or, simply, minimal factorization) of
L393@P7: a permutation π ∈ Sm, is a product σ1 · · · σn of a minimal number of
L394@P7: transpositions, such that π = σ1 · · · σn. In this section, the number of
L395@P7: geodesics between antipodes in Pm is shown to be equal to the number of minimal factorizations of an m-cycle in Sm. It follows from a
L396@P7: result of Hurwitz [9], as explained by Strehl [12], and Cayley’s classical
L397@P7: formula [5] that the latter number is the same as the number of labeled
L398@P7: trees on m vertices. Bijections which explain this coincidence directly
L399@P7: can be, e.g., found in [7, 11].
L400@P7: Throughout this section, the vertices of the underlying complete
L401@P7: graph K2m of Pm, are labeled by {1, −1, . . . , m, −m}. Denote the
L402@P7: complete bipartite graph with bipartition of vertices {1, . . . , m} and
L403@P7: {−1, . . . , −m} by Km,m. Denote the subgraph of Pm, induced by the
L404@P7: perfect matchings of Km,m, by Pm,m. Matchings in Pm,m correspond
L405@P7: naturally to permutations in Sm, by identifying a matching π ∈ Pm,m
L406@P7: with a permutation π
